name: Aisha Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how did you end up in this job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started in a warehouse at 19, picking orders, and the drivers always looked like they had the better deal. I did my truck licence at 22 and then the dangerous goods certificate, which is the extra licence you need to carry fuel. Now I drive a fuel tanker for a regional distributor, and the hazard pay is why my savings look healthy for someone my age.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the terminal by the docks at five, load 36,000 litres of diesel and petrol through the bottom valves, and run it out to petrol stations and a couple of big farms. I love that it's skilled and nobody hurries you. Every drop is the same careful routine: earth lead on, hoses checked, dipping the tanks before and after. You can't hurry fuel. What wears me out is the paperwork at every stop and the car drivers who cut in front of a full tanker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. Everyone at the terminal has been saying the robots are coming for years, and here we'd be, still dipping tanks by hand. Online I'd probably post something about how the money should have gone into safer roads instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I'm fine. I've got eleven months of rent and bills saved, I live on my own with my cat, and tanker drivers with the dangerous goods ticket are hard to find. If AI only takes some of the forms off me, that's a win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my union health and safety rep role, which I took on last spring. I already use a chatbot now and then to tidy up my safety reports, and I'd use it a bit more for that. Otherwise, same life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a little bored by how little changes. The fuel still needs moving and so do I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI could take some forms off you. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The delivery notes and the near-miss reports. Last month a van pulled out in front of me on the bypass, and writing it up properly took forty minutes at the end of a ten-hour day. A tanker driver should spend the day's energy on the valves, not on typing up near misses at nine at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you're worried about anyway, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electric cars. Fewer people buying petrol means fewer fuel runs in ten years, robots or no robots. That's why I keep the savings up and why I'd never buy a house that needs my full wage.

say: I'd joke that I **told you so**, because tanks still get dipped by hand.
I'd post that the money should have gone into **safer roads** instead.
think: Privately I'm **fine**, with eleven months saved and a scarce **dangerous goods ticket**.
Losing some **forms** to AI would be a win, not a threat.
do: Keep driving the tanker and stay on as **union safety rep**.
Use the **chatbot** a bit more to tidy up safety reports.
feel: **Calm**, maybe a little **bored** by how little changes.
S0.quote: A tanker driver should spend the day's energy on the valves, not on typing up near misses at nine at night.
fieldNote: Aisha's scarce **hazardous goods skill** gives her real security in a quiet world.
Her long-term worry is **electric cars** shrinking fuel demand, not AI.
She already uses a chatbot for **report writing**, which fits her steady adaptability.

steps.text: Keep driving the fuel tanker and the union safety rep role
Use a chatbot to draft near-miss and safety reports faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the software do the delivery notes, but keep a human in the cab with 36,000 litres of fuel. At union meetings I'd push for a say in which tools come in. Online I'd share stories about drivers whose jobs got worse, not better, with tracking apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a good spot for a while. My job is mostly hands-on and safety-critical, and the thinking bits are small. But the planners at our terminal would get squeezed, and they'll start timing us with software to the minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever planning app the company brings in, properly, so I can spot when it's wrong. Through the union I'd ask for a rule that no app can set a delivery time that breaks the rest-break laws. And I'd keep my savings growing, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of watchfulness. I've seen apps make jobs worse. I'd want to make sure this time drivers have a voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean when you say apps made jobs worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Kelly drives for a parcel firm, and the app gives Kelly a delivery slot every four minutes. If fuel planning went that way, a forecourt catches fire. Someone would rush a delivery, the way Kelly eats lunch at the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more yourself in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I've seen it work. I'd use it to read the new rules when they change, because the dangerous goods regulations are hundreds of pages. I wouldn't trust it to tell me a valve is closed, though.

say: I'd welcome software doing **delivery notes** but insist on a human with the fuel.
I'd share stories of drivers whose jobs got worse under **tracking apps**.
think: Privately my job is **safe for a while**, because it's hands-on and safety-critical.
The terminal's **planners** would get squeezed, and drivers would be timed to the minute.
do: Learn the company's new **planning app** well enough to spot its mistakes.
Push through the union for a rule protecting **rest breaks** from app schedules.
Keep my **savings** growing at the usual rate.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with some **watchfulness** about how apps get used on drivers.
S1.quote: My mate Kelly drives for a parcel firm, and the app gives Kelly a delivery slot every four minutes. If fuel planning went that way, a forecourt catches fire.
fieldNote: Aisha welcomes AI on paperwork but fears **app-driven schedules** that push drivers to rush.
Her concern is **safety and fairness**, not her own pay.
She'd learn tools to **check them**, a steady and practical stance.

steps.text: Learn the company's new fuel planning app inside out
Propose a union rule protecting rest breaks from app schedules
Use AI to look up changes in dangerous goods rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this is too fast for anyone to handle safely, and the companies should be made to slow down. At work I'd tell people to read their contracts and join the union if they haven't. Online I'd be one of those people sharing the petition every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my driving has about five years left, not three, because carrying fuel is so regulated that robot tankers would be among the last approved. But 'last' still means by my early thirties. I'd have savings and the dangerous goods ticket, but a dangerous goods ticket for a job robots do is worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up straight away for a gas and heating engineer course at the college, two evenings a week. Working inside people's homes, around their stairs and their dogs, seems like the last place robots go. I'd keep driving to pay for it and push more into savings, maybe an extra two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with a plan, which makes it bearable. I keep thinking about the 2031 date. I'd be 32, starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028 and robots in 2031. What changes for you in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office goes first, so the planners and the dispatchers, and probably the person who checks my tachograph, the machine that records my driving hours. I'd still be in the cab, but I'd be watching every trial of driverless tankers in the news. Those three years are my retraining window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. He was a bus driver for thirty years and got moved onto a desk job when they brought in automatic ticketing. He'd say don't wait, you won't get a second chance at the timing.

say: I'd say publicly that the change is **too fast** to handle safely.
I'd urge workmates to read contracts and **join the union**.
think: Privately my driving has **about five years** left, because fuel rules would slow robot tankers.
My **dangerous goods ticket** would be worthless once robots do the job.
do: Start a **gas and heating engineer** course at college, two evenings a week.
Keep driving to pay for it and save an **extra £200** a month.
Push workmates to join the **union** before the robots arrive.
feel: **Scared** but steadier for having a plan, picturing starting again at 32.
S2.quote: I'd have savings and the dangerous goods ticket, but a dangerous goods ticket for a job robots do is worth nothing.
fieldNote: Aisha treats the **three-year gap** between AGI and robots as her retraining window.
She expects to lose driving but holds **some control** through savings and a clear plan.
Her father's **bus-to-desk move** shapes her belief in acting early.

steps.text: Start a gas and heating engineer course two evenings a week
Save an extra £200 a month while still driving
Sign up workmates at the terminal to the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough warning that nobody should be caught out, so let's use it. At the union I'd push for the company to fund retraining instead of a payout at the end. Online I'd share the courses I find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years plus three before the robots means I'd have till about 2034, when I'm 35. That's time to finish a whole trade apprenticeship while still earning. I'm more worried for older drivers at the terminal than for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look into the heating engineer course and maybe start in September. I'd keep driving full time, keep saving, and use AI to help with the course theory, because I'm rubbish at maths. I'd wait a bit before quitting anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe a bit more than uneasy. The job I chose on purpose has an end date. But I've got time and money, and that's more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're worried for the older drivers. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a driver called Graham who's 61 and has never sent an email. He'd be 69 in 2034 and should have retired anyway. It's the ones in their forties with kids that I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'maybe start in September'. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years sounds like plenty, and the pay is good, and I'd tell myself next year. Getting comfortable is the honest risk.

say: I'd say five years is **enough warning** if people actually use it.
I'd push the union for **company-funded retraining** instead of an end payout.
think: Privately I'd have until about **2034**, enough to finish a trade while earning.
I worry more for **drivers in their forties** with kids than for myself.
do: Look into the **heating engineer course** and aim to start in September.
Keep driving full time and **keep saving**.
Use **AI** to help with the course theory, especially the maths.
feel: **Uneasy**, because a job chosen on purpose now has an **end date**.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like plenty, and the pay is good, and I'd tell myself next year. Getting comfortable is the honest risk.
fieldNote: Aisha still expects to lose driving, but **time and savings** give her real control.
She names her own **complacency** as the main danger.
Her concern for **mid-career colleagues** reflects her union outlook.

steps.text: Enrol in the heating engineer course for September
Use AI tutoring for the course maths and theory
Push the union for company-funded driver retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper chance to do this right, and if the government messes it up there's no excuse. At work I'd keep pushing the union to get a transition plan in writing. Online I'd tell people not to panic, but not to sleep either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's the most comfortable of the AGI pictures for me. Robots for hands-on work around 2039, when I'm 40, gives me a full career change with time to spare. Electric cars might take the fuel runs before the robots do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the tanker for a few more years and start the heating engineer course in the second or third year, not straight away. I'd put money aside for a van and tools. And I'd keep using AI for the boring writing, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a bit of unease underneath. A decade is a long time. I'd have a plan and a nest egg, and that's what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said electric cars might take the runs first. Does that change your timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. If our terminal starts losing petrol stations, I'd move faster on the course. Fuel was always a shrinking business; AI just puts a date on the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young driver just starting out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the licence, earn the good money for five years, save hard, and learn a trade on the side. Don't buy the shiny car. My first year I bought a stupid car, and I'd tell any new driver to skip the shiny car and buy tools instead.

say: I'd say ten years is a **proper chance**, so failure would have **no excuse**.
I'd tell people online **not to panic** but not to sleep either.
think: Privately this is the **most comfortable** AGI picture for me.
**Electric cars** might take the fuel runs before the robots do anyway.
do: Keep driving the tanker and start the **heating course** in year two or three.
Save for a **van and tools** for the new trade.
S4.quote: Fuel was always a shrinking business; AI just puts a date on the robots.
fieldNote: Aisha sees the decade as **time to plan**, so her mood eases.
She links AI to an older threat, **electric cars**, which she already planned around.
Her advice to new drivers shows a **save-and-retrain** mindset.

steps.text: Keep driving the tanker for the next few years
Start the heating engineer course in year two or three
Save for a van and tools for the heating trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of me, I'd be all right in the end, but because nobody would have time to train for anything. What would help is the company paying for retraining while we still work, and a law that robots carrying fuel need the same safety checks I do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but a tanker is a bomb on wheels if it's handled badly. I'd want to know who inspects the robot before it pulls onto a forecourt full of families.

headlineQuote: Every drop is the same careful routine: earth lead on, hoses checked, dipping the tanks before and after. You can't hurry fuel.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old fuel tanker driver** with a scarce dangerous goods licence and eleven months saved.
She lives alone, is her terminal's **union safety rep**, and uses a chatbot now and then.
In the slower pictures she's **calm** and welcomes AI taking her paperwork.
Faster AGI makes her **anxious**, and she'd retrain as a **heating engineer** while still driving.
She cares most about **safety** on the road and about older colleagues.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nobody would have time to train for anything.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **retraining** while working, and a law holding robot tankers to driver **safety checks**.
